subject: Ward Protocols
title: Hyperkalemia Emergencies: ECG Clues, Calcium and Potassium Removal
preview: Learn why ECG findings matter, why calcium stabilizes the myocardium but does not remove potassium, and how to avoid missing pseudohyperkalemia.
body:
Hyperkalemia (K+ > 5.5 mEq/L) is a medical emergency that can lead to fatal arrhythmias. ECG Changes: Tall peaked T waves → Loss of P wave → Widened QRS → Sine wave pattern → Asystole.

Step 1: Stabilize the Myocardium (Most Urgent)
Administer IV Calcium Gluconate (or Calcium Chloride via central line). Note: Calcium does NOT lower serum potassium; it only protects the heart by raising the threshold potential.

Step 2: Shift Potassium Intracellularly
• IV Insulin (Regular) + 50% Dextrose (to prevent hypoglycemia).
• Salbutamol (Albuterol) nebulization (Beta-2 agonist).
• IV Sodium Bicarbonate (especially if the patient is acidotic).

Step 3: Excrete Potassium from the Body
• Loop diuretics (Furosemide).
• GI cation-exchange resins (Patiromer, Sodium Zirconium Cyclosilicate).
• Hemodialysis (the ultimate definitive treatment if refractory).

sections.title: Recognize the risk
points: Hyperkalemia is an elevated blood potassium concentration; severity depends on the level, rate of rise, symptoms and ECG findings.
Significant hyperkalemia may cause conduction abnormalities, malignant arrhythmias and cardiac arrest.
A normal or minimally abnormal ECG does not reliably rule out dangerous hyperkalemia.

sections.title: ECG patterns to recognize
points: Peaked T waves, prolonged PR interval, reduced P-wave amplitude, QRS widening and a sine-wave pattern are classic findings.
The ECG sequence is not obligatory; patients may lack classic changes despite significant hyperkalemia.

sections.title: Emergency logic: protect → shift → remove
points: Protect the myocardium with intravenous calcium when indicated by significant ECG abnormalities or the emergency pathway. Calcium does not meaningfully lower serum potassium.
Temporarily shift potassium into cells using therapies such as insulin with glucose and, in selected cases, beta-2 agonists; monitor blood glucose.
Remove potassium from the body and address the cause; renal replacement therapy may be required in severe or refractory cases.

sections.title: Exam trap: calcium is not potassium elimination
points: Calcium stabilizes cardiac excitability; insulin-glucose shifts potassium intracellularly; elimination requires kidney excretion, gastrointestinal removal or dialysis.
Do not delay urgent assessment while waiting for a textbook-perfect ECG pattern.

sections.title: Memory aid
points: Emergency hyperkalemia: protect the heart → shift potassium → remove potassium.
Calcium protects cardiac electrical stability but does not remove potassium.

sections.title: Pseudohyperkalemia and follow-up
points: Consider a hemolyzed sample or collection artifact when the result does not fit the clinical context.
Repeat the sample promptly when appropriate, while treating high-risk symptomatic or ECG-positive patients urgently.
Recheck potassium and glucose after therapy and monitor for rebound.

quiz.question: What is the immediate purpose of intravenous calcium in severe hyperkalemia with ECG abnormalities?
quiz.explanation: Calcium stabilizes cardiac electrical activity; it does not remove potassium.

quiz.question: Which ECG change is classically associated with advanced hyperkalemia?
options: Persistent narrow QRS as a rule
quiz.explanation: QRS widening and loss of P waves can appear as hyperkalemia progresses.

quiz.question: An unexpectedly high potassium level is reported from a visibly hemolyzed sample without concordant findings. What should be considered?
options: A definitive diagnosis of adrenal crisis
quiz.explanation: Hemolysis can artifactually raise measured potassium; assess the clinical urgency and repeat appropriately.

rapidRevision: Intravenous calcium protects cardiac conduction but does not lower serum potassium.
Insulin-glucose causes a temporary intracellular shift; definitive removal is still needed.
Severity and ECG findings are not perfectly correlated.
Consider sample hemolysis if the laboratory result is discordant.
